body.heading: A ruler for acidity
paragraphs: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a water-based liquid is, and it runs from 0 to 14. In the middle sits 7, the pH of pure water, which is neutral — neither acidic nor basic. Numbers below 7 are acids; numbers above 7 are bases, also called alkalis when they dissolve in water.

The scale hides a twist: it is logarithmic, meaning each step is ten times bigger than the last. Lemon juice at pH 2 is not slightly more acidic than a pH 4 tomato — it carries about a hundred times the concentration of hydrogen ions. Small steps on this ruler are big jumps in strength.

body.heading: From battery acid to soap
paragraphs: At the bottom of the scale, the acid inside a car battery sits near pH 0, and your stomach acid — strong enough to dissolve food — measures around 1.5 to 2. Lemon juice is near 2, vinegar around 2.5 to 3, and ordinary rainwater is mildly acidic at about 5.6, thanks to carbon dioxide dissolved from the air.

Crossing 7, the numbers climb through soap at around 9 to 10, household bleach near 13, and heavy-duty oven cleaner up at 14. The liquid in the middle of your day — drinking water, milk, blood — stays close to neutral, and blood is guarded especially tightly, at about 7.4.

body.heading: Why the number matters
paragraphs: pH quietly decides real outcomes. Swimming pools are kept near 7.2 to 7.8: too acidic and the water stings eyes, too basic and the disinfectant stops working well. Acid rain, made stronger by pollution, slowly eats limestone buildings and statues that stood for centuries.

Gardeners may know the prettiest demonstration: hydrangea flowers bloom blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, because the pH changes how the plant handles aluminium. One flower bed, two colours — set by a number on a scale.
